claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed framework integrates reduced-order microscale simulations with minimal experimental calibration.
Reduced-order simulations can capture local mechanical responses influenced by nanoscale heterogeneities in HfNbTiVAl10.
Targeted nanoindentation and small-scale tensile and fracture tests will be used to calibrate the surrogate.
The surrogate will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness within 10% of experimental values.
The surrogate will reduce computational effort by at least 10-fold relative to full-scale first-principles, CALPHAD, and other conventional high-fidelity methods.
The method remains valid from ambient to moderate temperatures when the hierarchical microstructure does not change and adverse phase transformations are absent.
Reliable predictions require calibration experiments that accurately represent local microstructural variation.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and the hierarchical heterostructure mediate local stress distributions.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and the hierarchical heterostructure mediate defect mobility.
The resulting local stress distributions and defect mobilities determine elastic and fracture behavior.
An adaptive data-driven surrogate can replace exhaustive simulations while retaining essential physics and microstructural heterogeneity.
The surrogate can map microstructural features to macroscopic mechanical responses.
Full CALPHAD, first-principles, and high-fidelity molecular-dynamics methods demand large computational resources.
Conventional computational methods struggle to predict fracture properties.
Reliability may decrease when high thermal exposure or prolonged loading causes the hierarchical structure to evolve.
The method may lose reliability when phase transformations absent from the calibration dataset emerge.
The claimed accuracy and speed gains depend on calibration quality and the representativeness of reduced-order simulation inputs.
The benchmark will compare predictions with measurements from standardized tensile and notched-fracture tests performed under identical conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if any predicted property differs from measurement by more than 10% or if computational time is not reduced by approximately 10-fold.
